title: What is Elasticsearch, and how does it search internally (inverted index, analyzers, sharding, near-real-time)?
shortTitle: What Elasticsearch is, and how it searches internally — inverted index, analyzers, sharding, near-real-time

s1_definition.profdef: Elasticsearch is a distributed, document-oriented search and analytics engine built on top of Apache Lucene. It stores data as JSON documents in indices and makes them searchable in near-real-time through four core mechanisms. The inverted index maps each term to the list of documents containing it, which is what makes full-text search fast. Analyzers transform text into normalized terms during both indexing and querying so that searches match regardless of case, punctuation, or word form. Sharding splits an index into pieces distributed across nodes so data and query load scale horizontally, with replicas providing redundancy. Near-real-time means a newly indexed document becomes searchable after a short refresh interval, typically one second, rather than instantly, because Lucene buffers writes and periodically makes them visible.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the back of a thick banking regulations manual at National Bank of India. Instead of reading every page to find the word "overdraft," you flip to the index at the back, which lists "overdraft" and the exact pages it appears on. That back-of-book index is an inverted index. The analyzer is the librarian who, before building that index, lowercases everything and ignores commas so "Overdraft," and "overdraft" land on the same entry. Sharding is splitting the enormous manual into ten volumes kept in ten different rooms so ten clerks can search at once. And near-real-time is the rule that a newly added page shows up in the index a second after it is filed, not the instant the ink dries.
s1_definition.oneliner: Elasticsearch flips the problem around — instead of scanning documents for a word, it keeps a word-to-documents map, splits it across machines, and refreshes it about once a second.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Elasticsearch is a distributed, document-oriented search and analytics engine built on top of Apache Lucene. It stores data as JSON documents in indices and makes them searchable in near-real-time through four core mechanisms. The inverted index maps each term to the list of documents containing it, which is what makes full-text search fast. Analyzers transform text into normalized terms during both indexing and querying so that searches match regardless of case, punctuation, or word form. Sharding splits an index into pieces distributed across nodes so data and query load scale horizontally, with replicas providing redundancy. Near-real-time means a newly indexed document becomes searchable after a short refresh interval, typically one second, rather than instantly, because Lucene buffers writes and periodically makes them visible.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the back of a thick banking regulations manual at National Bank of India. Instead of reading every page to find the word "overdraft," you flip to the index at the back, which lists "overdraft" and the exact pages it appears on. That back-of-book index is an inverted index. The analyzer is the librarian who, before building that index, lowercases everything and ignores commas so "Overdraft," and "overdraft" land on the same entry. Sharding is splitting the enormous manual into ten volumes kept in ten different rooms so ten clerks can search at once. And near-real-time is the rule that a newly added page shows up in the index a second after it is filed, not the instant the ink dries.

**One line to remember:** Elasticsearch flips the problem around — instead of scanning documents for a word, it keeps a word-to-documents map, splits it across machines, and refreshes it about once a second.

sections.s2_technical:
Elasticsearch stores data as JSON documents grouped into an index, which is roughly analogous to a table in a relational database but optimized for search rather than transactional updates. Each document has fields, and the mapping describes the type of each field. Under the hood every index is powered by Apache Lucene, and most of the clever search behaviour comes from Lucene; Elasticsearch adds the distributed layer, the REST API, and cluster management on top.

The inverted index is the foundational data structure. A normal, or forward, index would map each document to the words it contains. An inverted index does the reverse: it maps each unique term to the sorted list of documents that contain it, called a postings list, often with the positions of the term within each document. So to find all documents containing "overdraft," Elasticsearch does not scan every document; it looks up "overdraft" once in the term dictionary and reads the postings list. This is why search stays fast even across billions of documents, and it is the same principle as the index at the back of a book.

Analyzers decide what the terms in that inverted index actually are. When a text field is indexed, it passes through an analyzer composed of three stages. Character filters may strip or replace characters, for example removing HTML. A tokenizer breaks the text into tokens, typically splitting on whitespace and punctuation, so "overdraft protection" becomes the tokens "overdraft" and "protection." Token filters then normalize the tokens, commonly lowercasing them, removing stop words like "the," and sometimes stemming so "transferring" and "transferred" reduce to a common root "transfer." The crucial point is that the same analyzer runs at query time, so a user searching for "Transferred" is normalized to the same term that was stored, and the match succeeds. This is why full-text search feels forgiving of case and word form. For fields where you want exact matching, such as a status code or an account ID, you use the keyword type, which is not analyzed and is stored verbatim.

Sharding is how Elasticsearch scales horizontally and stays available. When you create an index you choose a number of primary shards; each shard is itself a complete, independent Lucene index holding a subset of the documents. Elasticsearch decides which shard a document belongs to by hashing its routing value, usually the document id, so documents spread evenly. Because each shard is independent, a search is sent to every shard in parallel, each returns its best matches, and the coordinating node merges them, which is how query throughput scales with the number of nodes. Replica shards are copies of primaries placed on different nodes; they provide fault tolerance, since if a node holding a primary fails a replica is promoted, and they also serve read traffic, increasing search capacity. The number of primary shards is fixed at index creation, which is why sizing shards appropriately up front matters.

Near-real-time search is a direct consequence of how Lucene handles writes. When you index a document it is first written to an in-memory buffer and to a durable transaction log called the translog for crash safety, but it is not yet searchable. Periodically, by default every second, a refresh operation takes the buffered documents and writes them into a new Lucene segment that becomes searchable. So there is a small delay, the refresh interval, between indexing a document and being able to find it. This design is a deliberate trade-off: batching writes into segments is far more efficient than making every single write immediately searchable, and a one-second delay is irrelevant for log search and analytics. Segments are immutable once written; updates and deletes are handled by marking old documents as deleted and writing new segments, and a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones and purges deleted documents.

The senior-level nuance is understanding the trade-offs this architecture implies. Elasticsearch is optimized for read-heavy search and analytics, not for the strong transactional consistency of a relational database; it offers no multi-document transactions and only near-real-time visibility. Choosing the right number of shards matters because too many small shards waste overhead while too few huge shards cannot be rebalanced or parallelized well. The analyzer choice determines search quality, and mismatched index-time and query-time analyzers are a classic cause of "why does my search return nothing." And because the inverted index plus segment model favours append and search over frequent single-document updates, Elasticsearch shines for logs, metrics, product catalogues, and full-text search, while the system of record for money stays in a transactional database.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the fraud and support teams need to search millions of transaction audit records by free text — for example finding every record mentioning "international wire" for a given account — far faster than a relational database scan allows.

Problem 1 — A support agent types "International Wire" but the stored text reads "international wire transfer." A literal, case-sensitive match would find nothing. This is exactly what analyzers solve: both the stored text and the query are lowercased and tokenized, so the terms line up and the match succeeds.

Problem 2 — There are millions of records, and scanning each one for the words is far too slow. This is exactly what the inverted index solves: each term points directly to the records that contain it, so the search reads a short postings list instead of every document.

Problem 3 — The volume is too large for one machine, and the team cannot afford downtime if a node fails. This is exactly what sharding and replicas solve: the index is split across shards for parallel search and copied to replicas for resilience.

To make this runnable without a real cluster, we will build a small program that models these internals. It will contain an `Analyzer` that lowercases and tokenizes text, an `InvertedIndex` mapping terms to document ids, a `Shard` that holds its own inverted index for a subset of documents, and a `SearchEngine` that routes documents to shards by hashing, queries all shards in parallel, and merges results. The demo indexes several transaction audit documents, then searches for a phrase to show how analysis plus the inverted index produce fast, forgiving matches across shards.
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
mini-search/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/search/
│   │   │   ├── SearchDemo.java                    (main class)
│   │   │   ├── analysis/
│   │   │   │   └── Analyzer.java                   (char filter+tokenizer+filters)
│   │   │   ├── index/
│   │   │   │   ├── Document.java                   (a JSON-like doc)
│   │   │   │   └── InvertedIndex.java              (term -> postings list)
│   │   │   ├── shard/
│   │   │   │   └── Shard.java                      (one Lucene-like shard)
│   │   │   └── engine/
│   │   │       └── SearchEngine.java               (routing + fan-out + merge)
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── application.yml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/search/
│           └── engine/
│               └── SearchEngineTest.java
```

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml — mirrors index settings you would send to Elasticsearch
index:
  name: transaction-audit
  number_of_shards: 3
  number_of_replicas: 1
  refresh_interval: 1s          # near-real-time visibility
  analyzer: standard            # lowercase + tokenize on non-letters
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build and run the model
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/mini-search-1.0.0.jar

# Equivalent real Elasticsearch calls:
curl -X PUT "localhost:9200/transaction-audit" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"settings":{"number_of_shards":3,"number_of_replicas":1}}'
curl -X GET "localhost:9200/transaction-audit/_search" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query":{"match":{"text":"International Wire"}}}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four transaction audit documents, two mentioning international wire transfers with different casing, indexed into a three-shard engine, then a search for the phrase "International Wire."

Step 1: Document TXN-1 is indexed. The engine hashes its id and takes the result modulo three to pick a shard, then hands the document to that shard. The shard's analyzer turns "International Wire transfer to London" into the terms international, wire, transfer, london, dropping the stop word "to," and adds TXN-1 to each of those terms' postings lists.

Step 2: TXN-2, TXN-3, and TXN-4 are indexed the same way. Routing by hash spreads them across the three shards. Note TXN-3's text "international wire incoming from Dubai" produces the same lowercased terms international and wire as TXN-1, even though TXN-1 used capitals, because the analyzer lowercases both.

Step 3: The search for "International Wire" begins. The query runs through the identical analyzer, producing the terms international and wire. This is the crucial step: because the query is analyzed with the same rules as the documents, the capitalized query terms become the same lowercased terms that were stored.

Step 4: The engine fans the query out to all three shards in parallel. Each shard looks up "international" and "wire" in its own inverted index and intersects the postings lists, returning only documents that contain both terms. Shards holding TXN-1 and TXN-3 return those ids; shards holding TXN-2 and TXN-4 return nothing because those documents lack both terms.

Step 5: The coordinating engine merges the per-shard results into one set. The final answer is TXN-1 and TXN-3 — exactly the two international wire records — found by reading short postings lists rather than scanning every document, and matched despite the difference in capitalization.

Final output:

```text
Oct 25, 2026 2:30:11 AM com.bank.search.engine.SearchEngine search
INFO: shard 0 matched [TXN-1]
INFO: shard 2 matched [TXN-3]
Oct 25, 2026 2:30:11 AM com.bank.search.SearchDemo main
INFO: query 'International Wire' matched docs = [TXN-1, TXN-3]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Indexing a document
    "International Wire transfer to London" (TXN-1)
      │
      ▼ Analyzer: char filter → tokenize → lowercase → drop stop words
    [international, wire, transfer, london]
      │ route: hash("TXN-1") % 3 = shard 0
      ▼
    Shard 0 inverted index:
      international → {TXN-1}
      wire         → {TXN-1}
      transfer     → {TXN-1}

  Searching "International Wire"
      │
      ▼ SAME Analyzer → [international, wire]
   fan-out to all shards in parallel
      ├─ shard 0: international{TXN-1} ∩ wire{TXN-1} = {TXN-1}
      ├─ shard 1: (none)
      └─ shard 2: international{TXN-3} ∩ wire{TXN-3} = {TXN-3}
      ▼ coordinating node merges
    result = {TXN-1, TXN-3}   ← matched despite capitalization, no full scan
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Elasticsearch is a distributed, document-oriented search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene. It stores data as JSON documents in indices and makes them searchable in near-real-time. Four internal mechanisms explain how it searches so fast. The first is the inverted index: rather than mapping each document to the words it contains, it maps each unique term to the sorted list of documents that contain it, so finding every record mentioning "overdraft" is a single lookup plus reading a short postings list, not a scan of every document. That is the same idea as the index at the back of a book, and it is why search stays fast across billions of records.

The second mechanism is analyzers, which decide what the terms in that index actually are. When text is indexed it passes through character filters, a tokenizer that splits it into tokens, and token filters that lowercase, remove stop words, and sometimes stem words to a common root. The critical detail is that the very same analyzer runs at query time, so a user searching "International Wire" is normalized to the same lowercased terms that were stored, and the match succeeds despite the difference in casing. For fields that need exact matching, like an account id or a status code, I use the keyword type, which is stored verbatim and not analyzed.

The third mechanism is sharding. An index is split into primary shards, each a complete independent Lucene index holding a subset of the documents, and Elasticsearch routes a document to a shard by hashing its id so data spreads evenly. A search is scattered to every shard in parallel and the results are gathered and merged, which is how query throughput scales with the number of nodes. Replica shards are copies on other nodes that provide fault tolerance and extra read capacity. The fourth mechanism is near-real-time: a newly indexed document is buffered and written to a durable translog, but only becomes searchable after a refresh, by default every second, because batching writes into immutable Lucene segments is far more efficient than making every single write instantly visible.

The judgement I bring to interviews is knowing where this architecture fits and where it does not. Elasticsearch is superb for read-heavy full-text search, logs, metrics, and analytics, but it offers no multi-document transactions and only near-real-time consistency, so at National Bank of India the system of record for money always stayed in a transactional database, while Elasticsearch powered the fraud and support teams' fast searching over millions of transaction audit records. I size shards deliberately because too many tiny shards waste overhead and too few giant ones cannot parallelize, and I keep index-time and query-time analyzers consistent, because a mismatch there is the classic reason a search mysteriously returns nothing.
